#### 13.3.5 Managing User Daemons <a href="#Managing-User-Daemons" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-shepherd-services_002c-for-users" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services shepherd)` module supports the definitions of per-user Shepherd services (see <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org/shepherd/latest/en/shepherd.html#Introduction" data-manual="shepherd">Introduction</a> in The GNU Shepherd Manual). You extend `home-shepherd-service-type` with new services; Guix Home then takes care of starting the `shepherd` daemon for you when you log in, which in turns starts the services you asked for.

Variable: **home-shepherd-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dshepherd_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The service type for the userland Shepherd, which allows one to manage long-running processes or one-shot tasks. User’s Shepherd is not an init process (PID 1), but almost all other information described in (see <a href="#Shepherd-Services" class="pxref">Shepherd Services</a>) is applicable here too.

This is the service type that extensions target when they want to create shepherd services (see <a href="#Service-Types-and-Services" class="pxref">Service Types and Services</a>, for an example). Each extension must pass a list of `<shepherd-service>`. Its value must be a `home-shepherd-configuration`, as described below.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-shepherd-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dshepherd_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This data type represents the Shepherd’s configuration.

`shepherd (default: ``shepherd``)`  
The Shepherd package to use.

`auto-start? (default: ``#t``)`  
Whether or not to start Shepherd on first login.

`daemonize? (default: ``#t``)`  
Whether or not to run Shepherd in the background.

`silent? (default: ``#t``)`  
When true, the `shepherd` process does not write anything to standard output when started automatically.

`services (default: ``'()``)`  
A list of `<shepherd-service>` to start. You should probably use the service extension mechanism instead (see <a href="#Shepherd-Services" class="pxref">Shepherd Services</a>).

<span id="index-timers_002c-per_002duser" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The Shepherd allows you to define *timers*, a special type of service that performs a given task periodically. Just like you can define timers at the system level (see <a href="#Scheduled-Job-Execution" class="pxref">Scheduled Job Execution</a>), you can do so in your home environment.

The example below defines a home environment where a Shepherd timer runs the `mkid` command twice per day (see <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/idutils/manual/idutils.html#mkid-invocation" data-manual="idutils">mkid invocation</a> in ID Database Utilities). It does so by extending `home-shepherd-service-type` with `simple-service`; the Shepherd timer itself is produced by the `shepherd-timer` procedure (see <a href="#shepherd_002dtimer_002dprocedure" class="pxref"><code class="code">shepherd-timer</code></a>), which is given the service name, a gexp specifying its schedule, and a gexp specifying the command to run.

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu) (guix)
             (gnu home services shepherd)
             (gnu packages code))

(define idutils-service
  ;; Index my 'doc' directory everyday at 12:15PM and 7:15PM.
  (simple-service
   'update-idutils-database home-shepherd-service-type
   (list (shepherd-timer '(update-idutils-database)
                         #~(calendar-event #:hours '(12 19)
                                           #:minutes '(15))
                         #~(#$(file-append idutils "/bin/mkid")
                            "doc")))))

(home-environment
  ;; ...
  (services (append (list idutils-service)
                    %base-home-services)))
```

See <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org/shepherd/latest/en/shepherd.html#Timers" data-manual="shepherd">Timers</a> in The GNU Shepherd Manual for more information on Shepherd timers.

<span id="index-log-rotation_002c-for-user-services" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The Shepherd also comes with a *log rotation service*, which compresses and then deletes old log files produced by services and daemons that it runs. This service is made available through `home-log-rotation-service-type` as described below.

Variable: **home-log-rotation-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dlog_002drotation_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for the user Shepherd log rotation service (see <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org/shepherd/latest/en/shepherd.html#Log-Rotation-Service" data-manual="shepherd">Log Rotation Service</a> in The GNU Shepherd Manual). Its value must be a `log-rotation-configuration` record, exactly as for its system-wide counterpart. See <a href="#log_002drotation_002dconfiguration" class="xref">log-rotation-configuration</a>, for its reference.

This service is part of `%base-home-services`.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-shepherd-transient-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dshepherd_002dtransient_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Variable: **home-shepherd-timer-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dshepherd_002dtimer_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
These are the `timer` and `transient` Shepherd services. The former lets you schedule command execution for later, while the latter can run commands in the background as a regular service.

See <a href="#shepherd_002dtransient_002dtimer_002dservices" class="xref">the system <code class="code">timer</code> and <code class="code">transient</code> services</a>, which are their Guix System counterparts, for more info.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.6 Secure Shell <a href="#Secure-Shell-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-secure-shell-client_002c-configuration" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SSH-client_002c-configuration" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The <a href="https://www.openssh.com" class="uref">OpenSSH package</a> includes a client, the `ssh` command, that allows you to connect to remote machines using the <span class="abbr acronym" title="secure shell">SSH</span> (secure shell) protocol. With the `(gnu home services ssh)` module, you can set up OpenSSH so that it works in a predictable fashion, almost independently of state on the local machine. To do that, you instantiate `home-openssh-service-type` in your Home configuration, as explained below.

Variable: **home-openssh-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dopenssh_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service to set up the OpenSSH client. It takes care of several things:

- providing a `~/.ssh/config` file based on your configuration so that `ssh` knows about hosts you regularly connect to and their associated parameters;
- providing a `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, which lists public keys that the local SSH server, `sshd`, may accept to connect to this user account;
- optionally providing a `~/.ssh/known_hosts` file so that `ssh` can authenticate hosts you connect to.

Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-openssh-service-type
         (home-openssh-configuration
          (hosts
           (list (openssh-host (name "ci.guix.gnu.org")
                               (user "charlie"))
                 (openssh-host (name "chbouib")
                               (host-name "chbouib.example.org")
                               (user "supercharlie")
                               (port 10022))))
          (authorized-keys (list (local-file "alice.pub")))))
```

The example above lists two hosts and their parameters. For instance, running `ssh chbouib` will automatically connect to `chbouib.example.org` on port 10022, logging in as user ‘`supercharlie`’. Further, it marks the public key in `alice.pub` as authorized for incoming connections.

The value associated with a `home-openssh-service-type` instance must be a `home-openssh-configuration` record, as describe below.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-openssh-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dopenssh_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the datatype representing the OpenSSH client and server configuration in one’s home environment. It contains the following fields:

`hosts` (default: `'()`)  
A list of `openssh-host` records specifying host names and associated connection parameters (see below). This host list goes into `~/.ssh/config`, which `ssh` reads at startup.

`known-hosts` (default: `*unspecified*`)  
This must be either:

- `*unspecified*`, in which case `home-openssh-service-type` leaves it up to `ssh` and to the user to maintain the list of known hosts at `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, or
- a list of file-like objects, in which case those are concatenated and emitted as `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.

The `~/.ssh/known_hosts` contains a list of host name/host key pairs that allow `ssh` to authenticate hosts you connect to and to detect possible impersonation attacks. By default, `ssh` updates it in a *TOFU, trust-on-first-use* fashion, meaning that it records the host’s key in that file the first time you connect to it. This behavior is preserved when `known-hosts` is set to `*unspecified*`.

If you instead provide a list of host keys upfront in the `known-hosts` field, your configuration becomes self-contained and stateless: it can be replicated elsewhere or at another point in time. Preparing this list can be relatively tedious though, which is why `*unspecified*` is kept as a default.

`known-hosts2` (default: `*unspecified*`)  
Either `*unspecified*` or a list of file-like objects containing known host keys. When specified, these files will be concatenated and installed as `~/.ssh/known_hosts2`. This allows for declaratively manage known hosts (stored in `known_hosts2`), while leaving the primary `known_hosts` file unmanaged by Guix.

The SSH client by default reads both `known-hosts` and `known-hosts2` for host key verification. If only `known-hosts2` is specified in Guix Home, `known_hosts` remains as a regular file that SSH can modify, while `known_hosts2` contains the declaratively managed host keys.

`authorized-keys` (default: `#false`)  
The default `#false` value means: Leave any `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file alone. Otherwise, this must be a list of file-like objects, each of which containing an SSH public key that should be authorized to connect to this machine.

Concretely, these files are concatenated and made available as `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. If an OpenSSH server, `sshd`, is running on this machine, then it *may* take this file into account: this is what `sshd` does by default, but be aware that it can also be configured to ignore it.

`add-keys-to-agent` (default: `no`)  
This string specifies whether keys should be automatically added to a running ssh-agent. If this option is set to `yes` and a key is loaded from a file, the key and its passphrase are added to the agent with the default lifetime, as if by `ssh-add`. If this option is set to `ask`, `ssh` will require confirmation. If this option is set to `confirm`, each use of the key must be confirmed. If this option is set to `no`, no keys are added to the agent. Alternately, this option may be specified as a time interval to specify the key’s lifetime in `ssh-agent`, after which it will automatically be removed. The argument must be `no`, `yes`, `confirm` (optionally followed by a time interval), `ask` or a time interval.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **openssh-host** <a href="#index-openssh_002dhost" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `openssh-host` fields are:

`name` (type: string)  
Name of this host declaration. A `openssh-host` must define only `name` or `match-criteria`. Use host-name `\"*\"` for top-level options.

`host-name` (type: maybe-string)  
Host name—e.g., `"foo.example.org"` or `"192.168.1.2"`.

`match-criteria` (type: maybe-match-criteria)  
When specified, this string denotes the set of hosts to which the entry applies, superseding the `host-name` field. Its first element must be all or one of `ssh-match-keywords`. The rest of the elements are arguments for the keyword, or other criteria. A `openssh-host` must define only `name` or `match-criteria`. Other host configuration options will apply to all hosts matching `match-criteria`.

`address-family` (type: maybe-address-family)  
Address family to use when connecting to this host: one of `AF_INET` (for IPv4 only), `AF_INET6` (for IPv6 only). Additionally, the field can be left unset to allow any address family.

`identity-file` (type: maybe-string)  
The identity file to use—e.g., `"/home/charlie/.ssh/id_ed25519"`.

`port` (type: maybe-natural-number)  
TCP port number to connect to.

`user` (type: maybe-string)  
User name on the remote host.

`forward-x11?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Whether to forward remote client connections to the local X11 graphical display.

`forward-x11-trusted?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Whether remote X11 clients have full access to the original X11 graphical display.

`forward-agent?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Whether the authentication agent (if any) is forwarded to the remote machine.

`compression?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Whether to compress data in transit.

`proxy` (type: maybe-proxy-command-or-jump-list)  
The command to use to connect to the server or a list of SSH hosts to jump through before connecting to the server. The field may be set to either a `proxy-command` or a list of `proxy-jump` records.

As an example, a `proxy-command` to connect via an HTTP proxy at 192.0.2.0 would be constructed with: `(proxy-command "nc -X connect -x 192.0.2.0:8080 %h %p")`.

Data Type: **proxy-jump** <a href="#index-proxy_002djump" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `proxy-jump` fields are:

`user` (type: maybe-string)  
User name on the remote host.

`host-name` (type: string)  
Host name—e.g., `foo.example.org` or `192.168.1.2`.

`port` (type: maybe-natural-number)  
TCP port number to connect to.

`host-key-algorithms` (type: maybe-string-list)  
The list of accepted host key algorithms—e.g., `'("ssh-ed25519")`.

`accepted-key-types` (type: maybe-string-list)  
The list of accepted user public key types.

`control-master` (type: maybe-symbol)  
Enables the sharing of multiple sessions over a single network connection. Acceptable values are `'no`, `'yes`, `'auto`, `'ask`, and `'autoask`.

`control-file-name` (type: maybe-string)  
The file name of the control socket used for connection sharing, or `"none"` to disable connection sharing.

`control-persist` (type: maybe-string)  
When used in conjunction with `control-master`, specifies that the master connection should remain open in the background (waiting for future client connections) after the initial client connection has been closed.

`sent-environment-variables` (type: maybe-env-list)  
Specifies which variables from the local environment should be sent to the server. The server must also support it, and the server must be configured to accept those environment variables.

`environment-variables` (type: maybe-string-alist)  
List of environment variables with corresponding values to send to the server, as an alist of strings of the form `'("``variable``" . "``value``")`. The server must also support it, and the server must be configured to accept those environment variables.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: raw-configuration-string)  
Extra content appended as-is to this `Host` block in `~/.ssh/config`.

<span id="index-Parcimonie_002c-Home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `parcimonie` service runs a daemon that slowly refreshes a GnuPG public key from a keyserver. It refreshes one key at a time; between every key update parcimonie sleeps a random amount of time, long enough for the previously used Tor circuit to expire. This process is meant to make it hard for an attacker to correlate the multiple key update.

As an example, here is how you would configure `parcimonie` to refresh the keys in your GnuPG keyring, as well as those keyrings created by Guix, such as when running `guix import`:

``` lisp
(service home-parcimonie-service-type
         (home-parcimonie-configuration
           (refresh-guix-keyrings? #t)))
```

This assumes that the Tor anonymous routing daemon is already running on your system. On Guix System, this can be achieved by setting up `tor-service-type` (see <a href="#Networking-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">tor-service-type</code></a>).

The service reference is given below.

Variable: **parcimonie-service-type** <a href="#index-parcimonie_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for `parcimonie` (<a href="https://salsa.debian.org/intrigeri/parcimonie" class="uref">Parcimonie’s web site</a>). Its value must be a `home-parcimonie-configuration`, as shown below.

<!-- -->

Data Table: **home-parcimonie-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dparcimonie_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-parcimonie-configuration` fields are:

`parcimonie` (default: `parcimonie`) (type: file-like)  
The parcimonie package to use.

`verbose?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to have more verbose logging from the service.

`gnupg-already-torified?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether GnuPG is already configured to pass all traffic through <a href="https://torproject.org" class="uref">Tor</a>.

`refresh-guix-keyrings?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Guix creates a few keyrings in the `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, such as when running `guix import` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-import" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix import</code></a>). Setting this to `#t` will also refresh any keyrings which Guix has created.

`extra-content` (default: `#f`) (type: raw-configuration-string)  
Raw content to add to the parcimonie command.

<span id="index-ssh_002dagent" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The <a href="https://www.openssh.com" class="uref">OpenSSH package</a> includes a daemon, the `ssh-agent` command, that manages keys to connect to remote machines using the <span class="abbr acronym" title="secure shell">SSH</span> (secure shell) protocol. With the `(gnu home services ssh)` service, you can configure the OpenSSH ssh-agent to run upon login. See <a href="#GNU-Privacy-Guard" class="xref"><code class="code">home-gpg-agent-service-type</code></a>, for an alternative to OpenSSH’s `ssh-agent`.

Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-ssh-agent-service-type
         (home-ssh-agent-configuration
          (extra-options '("-t" "1h30m"))))
```

Variable: **home-ssh-agent-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dssh_002dagent_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the `ssh-agent` home service, whose value is a `home-ssh-agent-configuration` object.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-ssh-agent-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dssh_002dagent_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-ssh-agent-configuration` fields are:

`openssh` (default: `openssh`) (type: file-like)  
The OpenSSH package to use.

`socket-directory` (default: `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR``/ssh-agent"`) (type: gexp)  
The directory to write the ssh-agent’s `socket` file.

`extra-options` (default: `'()`)  
Extra options will be passed to `ssh-agent`, please run `man ssh-agent` for more information.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.7 GNU Privacy Guard <a href="#GNU-Privacy-Guard-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-GNU-Privacy-Guard_002c-Home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-GPG_002c-Home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services gnupg)` module provides services that help you set up the GNU Privacy Guard, also known as GnuPG or GPG, in your home environment.

<span id="index-gpg_002dagent_002c-Home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SSH-agent_002c-with-gpg_002dagent" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `gpg-agent` service configures and sets up GPG’s agent, the program that is responsible for managing OpenPGP private keys and, optionally, OpenSSH (secure shell) private keys (see <a href="https://www.gnupg.org/documentation/manuals/gnupg/Invoking-GPG_002dAGENT.html#Invoking-GPG_002dAGENT" data-manual="gnupg">Invoking GPG-AGENT</a> in Using the GNU Privacy Guard).

As an example, here is how you would configure `gpg-agent` with SSH support such that it uses the Emacs-based Pinentry interface when prompting for a passphrase:

``` lisp
(service home-gpg-agent-service-type
         (home-gpg-agent-configuration
          (pinentry-program
           (file-append pinentry-emacs "/bin/pinentry-emacs"))
          (ssh-support? #t)))
```

The service reference is given below.

Variable: **home-gpg-agent-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dgpg_002dagent_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for `gpg-agent` (see <a href="https://www.gnupg.org/documentation/manuals/gnupg/Invoking-GPG_002dAGENT.html#Invoking-GPG_002dAGENT" data-manual="gnupg">Invoking GPG-AGENT</a> in Using the GNU Privacy Guard). Its value must be a `home-gpg-agent-configuration`, as shown below.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-gpg-agent-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dgpg_002dagent_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-gpg-agent-configuration` fields are:

`gnupg` (default: `gnupg`) (type: file-like)  
The GnuPG package to use.

`pinentry-program` (type: file-like)  
Pinentry program to use. Pinentry is a small user interface that `gpg-agent` delegates to anytime it needs user input for a passphrase or <span class="abbr acronym" title="personal identification number">PIN</span> (personal identification number) (see <a href="pinentry.html#Top" data-manual="pinentry">Using the PIN-Entry</a>).

`home` (default: `"~/.gnupg"`) (type: string)  
The GnuPG home directory, relative to `$HOME`. Defaults to `~/.gnupg`.

`ssh-support?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to enable <span class="abbr acronym" title="secure shell">SSH</span> (secure shell) support. When true, `gpg-agent` acts as a drop-in replacement for OpenSSH’s `ssh-agent` program, taking care of OpenSSH secret keys and directing passphrase requests to the chosen Pinentry program.

`default-cache-ttl` (default: `600`) (type: integer)  
Time a cache entry is valid, in seconds.

`max-cache-ttl` (default: `7200`) (type: integer)  
Maximum time a cache entry is valid, in seconds. After this time a cache entry will be expired even if it has been accessed recently.

`default-cache-ttl-ssh` (default: `1800`) (type: integer)  
Time a cache entry for SSH keys is valid, in seconds.

`max-cache-ttl-ssh` (default: `7200`) (type: integer)  
Maximum time a cache entry for SSH keys is valid, in seconds.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: raw-configuration-string)  
Raw content to add to the end of `gpg-agent.conf`.

`shepherd-requirement` (default: `()`) (type: list-of-symbols)  
List of services that should be started before this service.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.8 Desktop Home Services <a href="#Desktop-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services desktop)` module provides services that you may find useful on “desktop” systems running a graphical user environment such as Xorg.

<span id="index-X-Window_002c-for-Guix-Home-services" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-X11_002c-in-Guix-Home" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Variable: **home-x11-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dx11_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type representing the X Window graphical display server (also referred to as “X11”).

X Window is necessarily started by a system service; on Guix System, starting it is the responsibility of `gdm-service-type` and similar services (see <a href="#X-Window" class="pxref">X Window</a>). At the level of Guix Home, as an unprivileged user, we cannot start X Window; all we can do is check whether it is running. This is what this service does.

As a user, you probably don’t need to worry or explicitly instantiate `home-x11-service-type`. Services that require an X Window graphical display, such as `home-redshift-service-type` below, instantiate it and depend on its corresponding `x11-display` Shepherd service (see <a href="#Shepherd-Home-Service" class="pxref">Managing User Daemons</a>).

When X Window is running, the `x11-display` Shepherd service starts and sets the `DISPLAY` environment variable of the `shepherd` process, using its original value if it was already set; otherwise, it fails to start.

The service can also be forced to use a given value for `DISPLAY`, like so:

``` example-preformatted
herd start x11-display :3
```

In the example above, `x11-display` is instructed to set `DISPLAY` to `:3`.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-wayland-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dwayland_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type representing a Wayland compositor. It functions as an equivalent of `x11-service-type` for Wayland.

Wayland compositors are typically started by services like `gdm-service-type`, described in the system configuration, although they can also be specified as a Guix Home service or started manually by the user. This means that we cannot always rely on the Wayland compositor being managed by Guix Home to tell whether one is present; we must explicitly check for it. This is what this service does.

As a user, you probably don’t need to worry or explicitly instantiate `home-wayland-service-type`. Services that require a Wayland graphical display instantiate this service and depend on its corresponding `wayland-display` Shepherd service (see <a href="#Shepherd-Home-Service" class="pxref">Managing User Daemons</a>).

If you’re writing a Shepherd service that requires the presence of a Wayland compositor, you need to depend on this service to ensure Wayland is accessible from your service.

When the Wayland compositor is running, the `wayland-display` Shepherd service starts and sets the `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` environment variable of the `shepherd` process, using its original value if it was already set; otherwise, it fails to start.

The service can also be forced to use a given value for `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, like so:

``` example-preformatted
herd start wayland-display wayland-2
```

In the example above, `wayland-display` is instructed to set `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` to `wayland-2`.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-redshift-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dredshift_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for <a href="https://github.com/jonls/redshift" class="uref">Redshift</a>, a program that adjusts the display color temperature according to the time of day. Its associated value must be a `home-redshift-configuration` record, as shown below.

A typical configuration, where we manually specify the latitude and longitude, might look like this:

``` lisp
(service home-redshift-service-type
         (home-redshift-configuration
          (location-provider 'manual)
          (latitude 35.81)    ;northern hemisphere
          (longitude -0.80))) ;west of Greenwich
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-redshift-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dredshift_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-redshift-configuration` fields are:

`redshift` (default: `redshift`) (type: file-like)  
Redshift package to use.

`location-provider` (default: `geoclue2`) (type: symbol)  
Geolocation provider—`'manual` or `'geoclue2`. In the former case, you must also specify the `latitude` and `longitude` fields so Redshift can determine daytime at your place. In the latter case, the Geoclue system service must be running; it will be queried for location information.

`adjustment-method` (default: `randr`) (type: symbol)  
Color adjustment method.

`daytime-temperature` (default: `6500`) (type: integer)  
Daytime color temperature (kelvins).

`nighttime-temperature` (default: `4500`) (type: integer)  
Nighttime color temperature (kelvins).

`daytime-brightness` (type: maybe-inexact-number)  
Daytime screen brightness, between 0.1 and 1.0, or left unspecified.

`nighttime-brightness` (type: maybe-inexact-number)  
Nighttime screen brightness, between 0.1 and 1.0, or left unspecified.

`latitude` (type: maybe-inexact-number)  
Latitude, when `location-provider` is `'manual`.

`longitude` (type: maybe-inexact-number)  
Longitude, when `location-provider` is `'manual`.

`dawn-time` (type: maybe-string)  
Custom time for the transition from night to day in the morning—`"HH:MM"` format. When specified, solar elevation is not used to determine the daytime/nighttime period.

`dusk-time` (type: maybe-string)  
Likewise, custom time for the transition from day to night in the evening.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: raw-configuration-string)  
Extra content appended as-is to the Redshift configuration file. Run `man redshift` for more information about the configuration file format.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-dbus-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002ddbus_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for running a session-specific D-Bus, for unprivileged applications that require D-Bus to be running.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-dbus-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002ddbus_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The configuration record for `home-dbus-service-type`.

`dbus` (default: `dbus`)  
The package providing the `/bin/dbus-daemon` command.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-unclutter-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dunclutter_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for Unclutter, a program that runs on the background of an X11 session and detects when the X pointer hasn’t moved for a specified idle timeout, after which it hides the cursor so that you can focus on the text underneath. Its associated value must be a `home-unclutter-configuration` record, as shown below.

A typical configuration, where we manually specify the idle timeout (in seconds), might look like this:

``` lisp
(service home-unclutter-service-type
         (home-unclutter-configuration
          (idle-timeout 2)))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-unclutter-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dunclutter_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The configuration record for `home-unclutter-service-type`.

`unclutter` (default: `unclutter`) (type: file-like)  
Unclutter package to use.

`idle-timeout` (default: `5`) (type: integer)  
A timeout in seconds after which to hide cursor.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-xmodmap-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dxmodmap_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for the <a href="https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/app/xmodmap" class="uref">xmodmap</a> utility to modify keymaps and pointer button mappings under the Xorg display server. Its associated value must be a `home-xmodmap-configuration` record, as shown below.

The `key-map` field takes a list of objects, each of which is either a *statement* (a string) or an *assignment* (a pair of strings). As an example, the snippet below swaps around the <span class="kbd kbd">Caps_Lock</span> and the <span class="kbd kbd">Control_L</span> keys, by first removing the keysyms (on the right-hand side) from the corresponding modifier maps (on the left-hand side), re-assigning them by swapping each other out, and finally adding back the keysyms to the modifier maps.

``` lisp
(service home-xmodmap-service-type
         (home-xmodmap-configuration
          (key-map '(("remove Lock" . "Caps_Lock")
                     ("remove Control" . "Control_L")
                     ("keysym Control_L" . "Caps_Lock")
                     ("keysym Caps_Lock" . "Control_L")
                     ("add Lock" . "Caps_Lock")
                     ("add Control" . "Control_L")))))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-xmodmap-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dxmodmap_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The configuration record for `home-xmodmap-service-type`. Its available fields are:

`xmodmap` (default: `xmodmap`) (type: file-like)  
The `xmodmap` package to use.

`key-map` (default: `'()`) (type: list)  
The list of expressions to be read by `xmodmap` on service startup.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-startx-command-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dstartx_002dcommand_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Add `startx` to the home profile putting it onto `PATH`.

The value for this service is a `<xorg-configuration>` object which is passed to the `xorg-start-command-xinit` procedure producing the `startx` used. Default value is `(xorg-configuration)`.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-darkman-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002ddarkman_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for the <a href="https://gitlab.com/WhyNotHugo/darkman" class="uref">Darkman</a>, a program for dark-mode and light-mode transitions on Unix-like desktops. It invokes scripts in `$XDG_DATA_DIRS/dark-mode.d` at sundown, and invokes scripts in `$XDG_DATA_DIRS/light-mode.d` at sunrise. Darkman tries to determine the user’s current location from:

- The config file.
- The cache file from last time it ran.
- Using the system geoclue.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-darkman-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002ddarkman_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The configuration record for `home-darkman-service-type`. Its available fields are:

`darkman` (default: `darkman`) (type: file-like)  
The `darkman` package to use.

`latitude` (type: maybe-number)  
Latitude, used at startup or when `use-geoclue` is `#f`. More than one decimal point is generally not needed.

`longitude` (type: maybe-number)  
Longitude, used at startup or when `use-geoclue` is `#f`. More than one decimal point is generally not needed.

`use-geoclue` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to use a local geoclue instance to determine the current location. Setting this to false without explicitly setting latitude and longtitude disables automatic transitions entirely.

`dbus-server` (default: `#t`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to expose the current mode via darkman’s own D-Bus API.

`portal` (default: `#t`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to expose the current mode via the XDG settings portal D-Bus API.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-gcr-ssh-agent-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dgcr_002dssh_002dagent_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
GNOME Keyring used to be able to act as a wrapper over `ssh-agent`. It would display a graphical password entry dialog, including a checkbox to remember the password, which, if selected, would allow fully passwordless use of that key.

The SSH functionality is disabled by default in `gnome-keyring-daemon` builds since version <a href="https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-keyring/-/commit25c5a1982467802fa12c6852b03c57924553ba73" class="uref">1.46</a>. It has been <a href="https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gcr/-/merge_requests/67" class="uref">moved</a> into `gcr-ssh-agent`, which is part of the `gcr` package.

To enable the SSH agent functionality it is sufficient to add the following to your Home configuration.

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu home services gnome) ;for 'home-gcr-ssh-agent-service-type'
             ...)

(home-environment
  (services
    (list
      ...
      (service home-gcr-ssh-agent-service-type))))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **gcr-ssh-agent-configuration** <a href="#index-gcr_002dssh_002dagent_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The configuration record for `home-gcr-ssh-agent-service-type`. Its available fields are:

`package` (default: `gcr`) (type: package)  
The `gcr` package to use.

`log-file` (type: maybe-string)  
Where the service will write its logs. If unset, it defaults to `$HOME/.local/state/shepherd/gcr-ssh-agent.log`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.9 XDG Home Services <a href="#XDG-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services xdg)` module provides services related to XDG specifications for the desktop.

#### XDG User Directories <a href="#XDG-User-Directories" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Variable: **home-xdg-user-directories-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dxdg_002duser_002ddirectories_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This service sets the names of default user directories such as ‘`Downloads`’ and ‘`Documents`’. These settings are respected by most applications via `xdg-user-dirs`.

To disable a directory, set it to `"$HOME"`.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-xdg-user-directories-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dxdg_002duser_002ddirectories_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-xdg-user-directories-configuration` fields are:

`desktop` (default: `"$HOME/Desktop"`) (type: string)  
Default ‘`Desktop`’ directory, this is what you see on your background when using a desktop environment, e.g. KDE.

`documents` (default: `"$HOME/Documents"`) (type: string)  
Default directory to put documents like PDFs.

`download` (default: `"$HOME/Downloads"`) (type: string)  
Default directory downloaded files, this is where your Web-broser will put downloaded files in.

`music` (default: `"$HOME/Music"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for audio files.

`pictures` (default: `"$HOME/Pictures"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for pictures and images.

`projects` (default: `"$HOME/Projects"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for projects.

`publicshare` (default: `"$HOME/Public"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for shared files, which can be accessed by other users on local machine or via network.

`templates` (default: `"$HOME/Templates"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for templates. They can be used by graphical file manager or other apps for creating new files with some pre-populated content.

`videos` (default: `"$HOME/Videos"`) (type: string)  
Default directory for videos.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.10 Guix Home Services <a href="#Guix-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services guix)` module provides services for user-specific Guix configuration.

Variable: **home-channels-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dchannels_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for managing `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/guix/channels.scm`, the file that controls the channels received on `guix pull` (see <a href="#Channels" class="pxref">Channels</a>). Its associated value is a list of `channel` records, defined in the `(guix channels)` module.

Generally, it is better to extend this service than to directly configure it, as its default value is the default guix channel(s) defined by `%default-channels`. If you configure this service directly, be sure to include a guix channel. See <a href="#Specifying-Additional-Channels" class="xref">Specifying Additional Channels</a> and <a href="#Using-a-Custom-Guix-Channel" class="ref">Using a Custom Guix Channel</a> for more details.

A typical extension for adding a channel might look like this:

``` lisp
(simple-service 'variant-packages-service
                home-channels-service-type
                (list
                 (channel
                  (name 'variant-packages)
                  (url "https://example.org/variant-packages.git"))))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.11 Backup Services <a href="#Backup-Services" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services backup)` module offers services for backing up file system trees. For now, it provides the `home-restic-backup-service-type`.

With `home-restic-backup-service-type`, you can periodically back up directories and files with <a href="https://restic.net/" class="uref">Restic</a>, which supports end-to-end encryption and deduplication. Consider the following configuration:

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu home services backup) ;for 'restic-backup-job', 'home-restic-backup-service-type'
             (gnu packages sync)        ;for 'rclone'
             ...)

(home-environment

  (packages (list rclone    ;for use by restic
                  ...))
  (services
    (list
      ...
      (simple-service 'backup-jobs
                      home-restic-backup-service-type
                      (list (restic-backup-job
                              (name "remote-ftp")
                              (repository "rclone:remote-ftp:backup/restic")
                              (password-file "/home/alice/.restic")
                              ;; Every day at 23.
                              (schedule "0 23 * * *")
                              (files '("/home/alice/.restic"
                                       "/home/alice/.config/rclone"
                                       "/home/alice/Pictures"))))))))
```

In general it is preferable to extend the `home-restic-backup-service-type`, as shown in the example above. This is because it takes care of wrapping everything with `for-home`, which enables the `home-restic-backup-service-type` and `restic-backup-service-type` to share the same codebase.

For a custom configuration, wrap your `restic-backup-configuration` in `for-home`, as in this example:

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu services)             ;for 'for-home'
             (gnu services backup)      ;for 'restic-backup-job' and 'restic-backup-configuration'
             (gnu home services backup) ;for 'home-restic-backup-service-type'
             (gnu packages sync)        ;for 'rclone'
             ...)

(home-environment

  (packages (list rclone    ;for use by restic
                  ...))
  (services
    (list
      ...
      (service home-restic-backup-service-type
               (for-home
                (restic-backup-configuration
                 (jobs (list ...))))))))
```

You can refer to see <a href="#Miscellaneous-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">restic-backup-service-type</code></a> for details about `restic-backup-configuration` and `restic-backup-job`. The only difference is that the `home-restic-backup-service-type` will ignore the `user` and `group` field of `restic-backup-job`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.12 Fonts Home Services <a href="#Fonts-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services fontutils)` module provides services for user-specific Fontconfig setup. The <a href="https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/fontconfig" class="uref">Fontconfig</a> library is used by many applications to access fonts on the system.

Variable: **home-fontconfig-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dfontconfig_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for generating configurations for Fontconfig. Its associated value is a list of either strings (or gexps) pointing to fonts locations, or SXML (see <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org/guile/latest/en/guile.html#SXML" data-manual="guile">SXML</a> in GNU Guile Reference Manual) fragments to be converted into XML and put inside the main `fontconfig` node.

Generally, it is better to extend this service than to directly configure it, as its default value is the default Guix Home’s profile font installation path (`~/.guix-home/profile/share/fonts`). If you configure this service directly, be sure to include the above directory.

Here’s how you’d extend it to include fonts installed with the Nix package manager, and to prefer your favourite monospace font:

``` lisp
(simple-service 'additional-fonts-service
                home-fontconfig-service-type
                (list "~/.nix-profile/share/fonts"
                      '(alias
                        (family "monospace")
                        (prefer
                         (family "Liberation Mono")))))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.13 Sound Home Services <a href="#Sound-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services sound)` module provides services related to sound support.

<span id="index-PulseAudio_002c-home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RTP_002c-for-PulseAudio" class="index-entry-id"></span>

#### PulseAudio RTP Streaming Services <a href="#PulseAudio-RTP-Streaming-Services" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The following services dynamically reconfigure the <a href="https://pulseaudio.org" class="uref">PulseAudio sound server</a>: they let you toggle broadcast of audio output over the network using the <span class="abbr acronym" title="real-time transport protocol">RTP</span> (real-time transport protocol) and, correspondingly, playback of sound received over RTP. Once `home-pulseaudio-rtp-sink-service-type` is among your home services, you can start broadcasting audio output by running this command:

``` example-preformatted
herd start pulseaudio-rtp-sink
```

You can then run a PulseAudio-capable mixer, such as `pavucontrol` or `pulsemixer` (both from the same-named package) to control which audio stream(s) should be sent to the RTP “sink”.

By default, audio is broadcasted to a multicast address: any device on the <span class="abbr acronym" title="local area network">LAN</span> (local area network) receives it and may play it. Using multicast in this way puts a lot of pressure on the network and degrades its performance, so you may instead prefer sending to specifically one device. The first way to do that is by specifying the IP address of the target device when starting the service:

``` example-preformatted
herd start pulseaudio-rtp-sink 192.168.1.42
```

The other option is to specify this IP address as the one to use by default in your home environment configuration:

``` lisp
(service home-pulseaudio-rtp-sink-service-type
         "192.168.1.42")
```

On the device where you intend to receive and play the RTP stream, you can use `home-pulseaudio-rtp-source-service-type`, like so:

``` lisp
(service home-pulseaudio-rtp-source-service-type)
```

This will then let you start the receiving module for PulseAudio:

``` example-preformatted
herd start pulseaudio-rtp-source
```

Again, by default it will listen on the multicast address. If, instead, you’d like it to listen for direct incoming connections, you can do that by running:

``` lisp
(service home-pulseaudio-rtp-source-service-type
         "0.0.0.0")
```

The reference of these services is given below.

Variable: **home-pulseaudio-rtp-sink-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dpulseaudio_002drtp_002dsink_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Variable: **home-pulseaudio-rtp-source-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dpulseaudio_002drtp_002dsource_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service to send, respectively receive, audio streams over <span class="abbr acronym" title="real-time transport protocol">RTP</span> (real-time transport protocol).

The value associated with this service is the IP address (a string) where to send, respectively receive, the audio stream. By default, audio is sent/received on multicast address `%pulseaudio-rtp-multicast-address`.

This service defines one Shepherd service: `pulseaudio-rtp-sink`, respectively `pulseaudio-rtp-source`. The service is not started by default, so you have to explicitly start it when you want to turn it on, as in this example:

``` example-preformatted
herd start pulseaudio-rtp-sink
```

Stopping the Shepherd service turns off broadcasting.

<!-- -->

Variable: **%pulseaudio-rtp-multicast-address** <a href="#index-_0025pulseaudio_002drtp_002dmulticast_002daddress" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the multicast address used by default by the two services above.

<span id="index-PipeWire_002c-home-service" class="index-entry-id"></span>

#### PipeWire Home Service <a href="#PipeWire-Home-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<a href="https://pipewire.org" class="uref">PipeWire</a> provides a low-latency, graph-based audio and video processing service. In addition to its native protocol, it can also be used as a replacement for both JACK and PulseAudio.

While PipeWire provides the media processing and API, it does not, directly, know about devices such as sound cards, nor how you might want to connect applications, hardware, and media processing filters. Instead, PipeWire relies on a *session manager* to specify all these relationships. While you may use any session manager you wish, for most people the <a href="https://pipewire.pages.freedesktop.org/wireplumber/" class="url">WirePlumber</a> session manager, a reference implementation provided by the PipeWire project itself, suffices, and that is the one `home-pipewire-service-type` uses.

PipeWire can be used as a replacement for PulseAudio by setting `enable-pulseaudio?` to `#t` in `home-pipewire-configuration`, so that existing PulseAudio clients may use it without any further configuration.

In addition, JACK clients may connect to PipeWire by using the `pw-jack` program, which comes with PipeWire. Simply prefix the command with `pw-jack` when you run it, and audio data should go through PipeWire:

``` example-preformatted
pw-jack mpv -ao=jack sound-file.wav
```

For more information on PulseAudio emulation, see <a href="https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/pipewire/pipewire/-/wikis/Config-PulseAudio" class="uref">https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/pipewire/pipewire/-/wikis/Config-PulseAudio</a>, for JACK, see <a href="https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/pipewire/pipewire/-/wikis/Config-JACK" class="uref">https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/pipewire/pipewire/-/wikis/Config-JACK</a>.

As PipeWire does not use `dbus` to start its services on demand (as PulseAudio does), `home-pipewire-service-type` uses Shepherd to start services when logged in, provisioning the `pipewire`, `wireplumber`, and, if configured, `pipewire-pulseaudio` services. See <a href="#Shepherd-Home-Service" class="xref">Managing User Daemons</a>.

Variable: **home-pipewire-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dpipewire_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This provides the service definition for `pipewire`, which will run on login. Its value is a `home-pipewire-configuration` object.

To start the service, add it to the `service` field of your `home-environment`, such as:

``` lisp
(service home-pipewire-service-type)
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-pipewire-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dpipewire_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-pipewire-configuration` fields are:

`pipewire` (default: `pipewire`) (type: file-like)  
The PipeWire package to use.

`wireplumber` (default: `wireplumber`) (type: file-like)  
The WirePlumber package to use.

`enable-pulseaudio?` (default: `#t`) (type: boolean)  
When true, enable PipeWire’s PulseAudio emulation support, allowing PulseAudio clients to use PipeWire transparently.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: string)  
Extra content to add to the end of `~/.config/alsa/asoundrc`.

#### 13.3.14 Mail Home Services <a href="#Mail-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services mail)` module provides services that help you set up the tools to work with emails in your home environment.

#### MSMTP Service <a href="#MSMTP-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-msmtp" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-mail-configuration_002c-for-outgoing-mail" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<a href="https://marlam.de/msmtp" class="uref">MSMTP</a> is a <span class="abbr acronym" title="Simple Mail
Transfer Protocol">SMTP</span> (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) client. It sends mail to a predefined SMTP server that takes care of proper delivery.

The service reference is given below.

Variable: **home-msmtp-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dmsmtp_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for `msmtp`. Its value must be a `home-msmtp-configuration`, as shown below. It provides the `~/.config/msmtp/config` file.

As an example, here is how you would configure `msmtp` for a single account:

``` lisp
(service home-msmtp-service-type
         (home-msmtp-configuration
          (accounts
           (list
            (msmtp-account
             (name "alice")
             (configuration
              (msmtp-configuration
               (host "mail.example.org")
               (port 587)
               (user "alice")
               (password-eval "pass Mail/alice"))))))))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-msmtp-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dmsmtp_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-msmtp-configuration` fields are:

`defaults` (type: msmtp-configuration)  
The configuration that will be set as default for all accounts.

`accounts` (default: `'()`) (type: list-of-msmtp-accounts)  
A list of `msmtp-account` records which contain information about all your accounts.

`default-account` (type: maybe-string)  
Set the default account.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: string)  
Extra content appended as-is to the configuration file. Run `man msmtp` for more information about the configuration file format.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **msmtp-account** <a href="#index-msmtp_002daccount" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `msmtp-account` fields are:

`name` (type: string)  
The unique name of the account.

`configuration` (type: msmtp-configuration)  
The configuration for this given account.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **msmtp-configuration** <a href="#index-msmtp_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `msmtp-configuration` fields are:

`auth?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Enable or disable authentication.

`tls?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Enable or disable TLS (also known as SSL) for secured connections.

`tls-starttls?` (type: maybe-boolean)  
Choose the TLS variant: start TLS from within the session (‘on’, default), or tunnel the session through TLS (‘off’).

`tls-trust-file` (type: maybe-string)  
Activate server certificate verification using a list of trusted Certification Authorities (CAs).

`log-file` (type: maybe-string)  
Enable logging to the specified file. An empty argument disables logging. The file name ‘-’ directs the log information to standard output.

`host` (type: maybe-string)  
The SMTP server to send the mail to.

`port` (type: maybe-integer)  
The port that the SMTP server listens on. The default is 25 ("smtp"), unless TLS without STARTTLS is used, in which case it is 465 ("smtps").

`user` (type: maybe-string)  
Set the user name for authentication.

`from` (type: maybe-string)  
Set the envelope-from address.

`password-eval` (type: maybe-string)  
Set the password for authentication to the output (stdout) of the command cmd.

`extra-content` (default: `""`) (type: string)  
Extra content appended as-is to the configuration block. Run `man msmtp` for more information about the configuration file format.

#### Goimapnotify Service <a href="#Goimapnotify-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-IMAP-notifications" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Variable: **home-goimapnotify-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dgoimapnotify_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service that runs <a href="https://gitlab.com/shackra/goimapnotify" class="uref">Goimapnotify</a>, a command-line application to execute scripts on IMAP mailbox changes using <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2177" class="uref">IDLE</a>. Its value is a `home-goimapnotify-configuration` object.

Here is a snippet of the service with an example configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-goimapnotify-service-type
         (home-goimapnotify-configuration
          (configurations
           (list
            (goimapnotify-configuration
             (host "imap.example.com")
             (tls? #t)
             (tls-options
              (goimapnotify-tls-options-configuration
               (reject-unauthorized? #t)))
             (user-name "alice@example.com")
             (password-command
              #~(string-append #$(file-append libsecret "/bin/secret-tool")
                               " lookup user alice@example.com"))
             (boxes
              (list
               (goimapnotify-box-configuration
                (mailbox "Inbox")
                (on-new-mail
                 #~(string-append #$(file-append isync "/bin/mbsync")
                                  " alice"))
                (on-new-mail-post
                 #~(string-append #$(file-append notmuch "/bin/notmuch")
                                  " new"))))))))))
```

Data Type: **home-goimapnotify-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dgoimapnotify_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-goimapnotify-configuration` fields are:

`goimapnotify` (default: `goimapnotify`) (type: file-like)  
The `goimapnotify` package to use.

`configurations` (type: list-of-goimapnotify-configurations)  
A list of `goimapnotify-configuration` records which contain information about all your accounts configurations.

`shepherd-requirement` (default: `()`) (type: list-of-symbols)  
A list of services that should be started before this service. For example, to make the service start after the gpg-agent service, (see <a href="#GNU-Privacy-Guard" class="pxref">GNU Privacy Guard</a>), one could write the following:

``` lisp
(shepherd-requirement '(gpg-agent))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **goimapnotify-configuration** <a href="#index-goimapnotify_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `goimapnotify-configuration` fields are:

`host` (type: string)  
The IMAP server hostname.

`host-command` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to retrieve the IMAP server hostname.

`port` (default: `993`) (type: integer)  
The port that the IMAP server listens on.

`tls?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Enable or disable TLS.

`tls-options` (type: maybe-goimapnotify-tls-options-configuration)  
TLS options for the IMAP connection.

`idle-logout-timeout` (type: maybe-integer)  
The idle logout timeout in minutes.

`user-name` (type: maybe-string)  
The user-name for authentication.

`user-name-command` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to retrieve the user-name.

`alias` (type: maybe-string)  
An alias for the account.

`password` (type: maybe-string)  
The password for authentication.

`password-command` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to retrieve the password.

`xo-auth2?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Enable or disable XOAUTH2 authentication.

`wait` (type: maybe-integer)  
The delay in seconds before the mail syncing is triggered.

`boxes` (type: list-of-goimapnotify-boxes-configurations)  
The mailboxes to monitor.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **goimapnotify-box-configuration** <a href="#index-goimapnotify_002dbox_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `goimapnotify-box-configuration` fields are:

`mailbox` (type: string)  
The mailbox to monitor.

`on-new-mail` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute when new mail arrives.

`on-new-mail-post` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute after the new-mail command.

`on-changed-mail` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute when mail is changed.

`on-changed-mail-post` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute after the changed-mail command.

`on-deleted-mail` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute when mail is deleted.

`on-deleted-mail-post` (type: maybe-string-or-gexp)  
The command to execute after the deleted-mail command.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **goimapnotify-tls-options-configuration** <a href="#index-goimapnotify_002dtls_002doptions_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `goimapnotify-tls-options-configuration` fields are:

`reject-unauthorized?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to reject unauthorized TLS certificates.

`starttls?` (default: `#f`) (type: boolean)  
Whether to use STARTTLS.

#### 13.3.15 Messaging Home Services <a href="#Messaging-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-znc" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The <a href="https://znc.in" class="uref">ZNC bouncer</a> can be run as a daemon to manage your IRC presence. With the `(gnu home services messaging)` service, you can configure ZNC to run upon login.

You will have to provide a `~/.znc/configs/znc.conf` separately.

Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-znc-service-type)
```

Variable: **home-znc-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dznc_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the ZNC home service, whose value is a `home-znc-configuration` object.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-znc-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dznc_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-znc-configuration` fields are:

`znc` (default: `znc`) (type: file-like)  
The ZNC package to use.

`extra-options` (default: `'()`)  
Extra options will be passed to `znc`, please run `man znc` for more information.

<span id="index-irc_002dbot-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-snuik-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The <a href="https://gitlab.com/janneke/snuik" class="uref">Snuik IRC bot</a> can be run as a daemon to aid talking to users that are currently offline. With the `(gnu home services messaging)` service, you can configure Snuik to run upon login.

Variable: **home-snuik-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dsnuik_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the Snuik home service, whose value is a `home-snuik-configuration` object.

You may specify a custom configuration by providing a `snuik-configuration` record, exactly like for `snuik-service-type` and wrapping it in `for-home`. Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-snuik-service-type
         (for-home
          (snuik-configuration
           (server "irc.oftc.net")
           (nick "sneek")
           (password "snuik is sneeky")
           (channels '("#reproducible-builds")))))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.16 Media Home Services <a href="#Media-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-kodi" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The <a href="https://kodi.tv" class="uref">Kodi media center</a> can be run as a daemon on a media server. With the `(gnu home services kodi)` service, you can configure Kodi to run upon login.

Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-kodi-service-type
  (home-kodi-configuration
   (extra-options '("--settings="<settings-file>"))))
```

Variable: **home-kodi-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dkodi_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the Kodi home service, whose value is a `home-kodi-configuration` object.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-kodi-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dkodi_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-kodi-configuration` fields are:

`kodi` (default: `kodi`) (type: file-like)  
The Kodi package to use.

`extra-options` (default: `'()`)  
Extra options will be passed to `kodi`, please run `man kodi` for more information.

#### 13.3.17 mpv Media Player <a href="#mpv-Media-Player-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-mpv_002c-Home-Service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-mpv_002c-configuration" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Configuring the <a href="https://mpv.io/" class="uref">mpv media player</a> can be somewhat daunting task, due to the sheer amount of options available, especially if one wants to be able to inherit the configuration in their code. The `home-mpv-service-type` is provided to help with that problem. When the service is added to your home environment, file based on the passed configuration is generated and placed into the correct location.

Due to the bug \#74748, it does not use Guix Records to represent the configuration, but uses keyword arguments to achieve similar result. Example follows:

``` lisp
(service home-mpv-service-type
         (make-home-mpv-configuration
          #:global (make-mpv-profile-configuration
                    #:fullscreen? #t
                    #:alang '("jpn" "eng"))))
```

Variable: **home-mpv-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dmpv_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the mpv home service, whose value is a `home-mpv-configuration` object.

<!-- -->

Procedure: **make-home-mpv-configuration** <a href="#index-make_002dhome_002dmpv_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Return a new instance of `home-mpv-configuration`. Available keyword arguments are:

`inherit` (default: `#t`)  
Inherit fields from an another instance.

`global` (default: `(make-mpv-profile-configuration)`)  
The global configuration preceding all profiles.

`profiles` (default: `()`)  
An alist containing configuration for any additional profiles to include in the configuration file.

``` lisp
(make-home-mpv-configuration
 #:profiles `((fullscreen . ,(make-mpv-profile-configuration
                              #:fullscreen? #t))))
```

`extra-config` (default: `#f`)  
Additional content to include in the configuration file. It is placed at the end of the file.

<!-- -->

Procedure: **make-mpv-profile-configuration** <a href="#index-make_002dmpv_002dprofile_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Return a new instance of `mpv-profile-configuration`. As above, it also supports the `#:inherit` argument. Additionally it supports keyword arguments named after the options of `mpv`. Hence `--fullscreen` (or `fullscreen` in the configuration file) becomes `#:fullscreen?`.

Few options are using their aliases instead. `audio` instead of `aid`, `video` instead of `vid`, `sub` instead of `sid`, `screenshot-directory` instead of `screenshot-dir` and `watch-later-directory` instead of `watch-later-dir`.

Valid values for the fields depend on their type.

Flags  
The value should be `#f` or `#t`.

Numerical fields  
Integer and integer64 fields are validated by `integer?`, float and double fields by `real?`. Ranges are checked when applicable.

Aspect  
Same as integer.

ByteSize  
Same as integer64.

Choice  
The value should be a symbol representing member of the enumeration. If the choice has ‘`or ...`’ part, it can also be value of that alternative type.

`type` list  
The value should be a list of the `type`.

Other types accept strings, with validation of the values where possible (e.g. type ‘`Color`’ is validated, but type ‘`Audio channels or channel map`’ is not). If an option is marked as taking a file, values satisfying `file-like?` can also be used.

The full list of currently supported keyword arguments is below. For the types, allowed values and full description please refer to the `mpv --list-options` and <a href="https://mpv.io/manual/stable/#options" class="uref">mpv manual</a>.

Only set fields are output to the configuration file. Accessors are provided for every field, returning either their value or a sentinel object `%unset-value` (from `(gnu services configuration)`).
