#### 13.3.18 Niri window manager <a href="#Niri-window-manager-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-niri_002c-Home-Service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-niri_002c-configuration" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Wayland-compositor" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-scrollable-tiling-window-manager" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services niri)` module provides the `home-niri-service-type` service, which installs and configures <a href="https://github.com/YaLTeR/niri" class="uref">Niri</a>, a scrollable tiling Wayland compositor. Niri combines traditional tiling window management with smooth scrolling between workspaces.

This service starts Niri as a user-level desktop session with proper environment variables configured for Wayland compatibility, including `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP`, `XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP`, and `DESKTOP_SESSION`.

Here is a minimal example service declaration for your `home-environment` configuration:

``` example-preformatted
(service home-niri-service-type)
```

For more advanced configurations, you can customize the service with a `niri-configuration` record to specify additional environment variables.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.19 Sway window manager <a href="#Sway-window-manager-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-sway_002c-Home-Service" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-sway_002c-configuration" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services sway)` module provides `home-sway-service-type`, a home service to configure the <a href="https://github.com/swaywm/sway" class="uref">Sway window manager for Wayland</a> in a declarative way.

Here is an example of a service and its configuration that you could add to the `services` field of your `home-environment`:

``` lisp
(service home-sway-service-type
         (sway-configuration
          (gestures
           '((swipe:3:down . "move to scratchpad")
             (swipe:3:up   . "scratchpad show")))
          (outputs
           (list (sway-output
                  (identifier '*)
                  (background (file-append sway
                                           "\
/share/backgrounds/sway/Sway_Wallpaper_Blue_1920x1080.png")))))))
```

The above example describes a Sway configuration in which

- all monitors use a particular wallpaper whose `.png` is provided by the `sway` package;
- swiping down (resp. up) with three fingers moves the active window to the scratchpad (resp. shows/hides the scratchpad).

> **Note:** This home service only sets up the configuration file and profile packages for Sway. It does *not* start Sway in any way. If you want to do so, you might be interested in using `greetd-wlgreet-sway-session` instead.
>
> The procedure `sway-configuration->file` defined below can be used to provide the value for the *optional* `sway-configuration` field of `greetd-wlgreet-sway-session`.

Procedure: **sway-configuration-\>file** `config` <a href="#index-sway_002dconfiguration_002d_003efile" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This procedure takes one argument `config`, which must be a `sway-configuration` record (defined below), and returns a file-like object representing the serialized configuration.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-sway-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dsway_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is a home service type to set up Sway. It takes care of:

- providing a `~/.config/sway/config` file,
- adding Sway-related packages to your profile.

It is possible to extend this service (see <a href="#Service-Composition" class="pxref">Service Composition</a>). The resulting configuration file contains the concatenation of keybindings, modes, *etc.* found in all extensions.

> **Note:** At the moment, only one bar configuration is allowed. If more are found, an error will be raised.

<!-- -->

Variable: **%empty-sway-configuration** <a href="#index-_0025empty_002dsway_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
The variable `%empty-sway-configuration` contains an empty `sway-configuration` record. This value can help users write simple service extensions.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-configuration** <a href="#index-sway_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This configuration record describes the Sway configuration (see sway(5)). Available fields are:

`variables` (default: `%sway-default-variables`)  
The value of this field is an association list in which keys are symbols and values are either strings, G-expressions or file-like objects (see <a href="#G_002dExpressions" class="pxref">G-Expressions</a>).

Example:

``` lisp
(variables `((mod . "Mod4") ; string
             (term ; file-append
              . ,(file-append foot "/bin/foot"))
             (Term ; G-expression
              . ,#~(string-append #$foot "/bin/foot"))))
```

> **Note:** Default keybindings assume the existence of variables named `$mod`, `$left`, `$right`, `$up` and `$down`. If you choose not to define these variables, make sure to remove keybindings referring to them.

`keybindings` (default: `%sway-default-keybindings`)  
This field describes keybindings for the *default* mode. The value is an association list in which keys are symbols. Values can either be:

- strings or G-expressions,
- a cons-cell of a string or G-expression and a list of options. Options must be a string starting with “input-device=” or strings among “no-warn”, “whole-window”, “border”, “exclude-titlebar”, “release”, “locked”, “to-code”, “inhibited” and “no-repeat”.

The following snippet launches the terminal when pressing <span class="kbd kbd">\$mod+t</span> and <span class="kbd kbd">\$mod+Shift+t</span> (assuming that a variable `$term` is defined):

``` lisp
`(($mod+t . ,#~(string-append "exec " #$foot "/bin/foot"))
  ($mod+Shift+t . "exec $term")
  ($mod+q "exec $term" . ("to-code"))) ;; passes the --to-code option.
```

`gestures` (default: `%sway-default-gestures`)  
Similar to the previous field, but for finger-gestures. Options must start with “input-device=” or be among “exact” and “no-warn”.

The following snippet allows to navigate through workspaces by swiping right and left with three fingers:

``` lisp
'((swipe:3:right . "workspace next_on_output")
  (swipe:3:left    "workspace prev_on_output" . ("exact")))
```

`packages` (default: `%sway-default-packages`)  
This field describes a list of packages to add to the user profile. At the moment, the default value only adds `sway` to the profile.

`inputs` (default: `'()`)  
List of `sway-input` configuration records (described below).

`outputs` (default: `'()`)  
List of `sway-output` configuration records (described below).

`bar` (optional `sway-bar` record)  
Optional `sway-bar` record (described below) to configure a Sway bar.

`modes` (default: `%sway-default-modes`)  
List of `sway-mode` records (described below) to add modes to the Sway configuration. The default value `%sway-default-modes` adds the “resize” mode of the default Sway configuration (as described below).

`startup+reload-programs` (default: `'()`)  
Programs to execute at startup time *and* after every configuration reload. The value of this field is a list of strings, G-expressions or file-like objects (see <a href="#G_002dExpressions" class="pxref">G-Expressions</a>).

`startup-programs` (default: `%sway-default-startup-programs`)  
Programs to execute at startup time. As above, values of this field are a list of strings, G-expressions or file-like objects.

The default value, `%sway-default-startup-programs`, executes `swayidle` in order to lock the screen after 5 minutes of inactivity (displaying a background distributed with Sway) and turn the screen off after 10 minutes of inactivity.

`extra-content` (default: `'()`)  
Lines to add to the configuration file. The value of this field is a list of strings or G-expressions.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-input** <a href="#index-sway_002dinput" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`sway-input` records describe input blocks (see sway-input(5)). For example, the following snippet makes all keyboards use a French layout, in which <span class="kbd kbd">capslock</span> has been remapped to <span class="kbd kbd">ctrl</span>:

``` lisp
(sway-input (identifier "type:keyboard")
            (layout
              (keyboard-layout "fr" #:options '("ctrl:nocaps"))))
```

Available fields for `sway-input` configuration records are:

`identifier` (default: `'*`)  
Identifier of the input. The field accepts symbols and strings. If the `identifier` is a symbol, it is inserted as is; if it is a string, it will be quoted in the configuration file.

`layout` (optional `<keyboard-layout>` record)  
Keyboard specific option. Field specifying the layout to use for the input. The value must be a `<keyboard-layout>` record (see <a href="#Keyboard-Layout" class="pxref">Keyboard Layout</a>).

> **Note:** `(gnu home services sway)` does not re-export the `keyboard-layout` procedure.

`disable-while-typing` (optional boolean)  
If `#t` (resp. `#f`) enables (resp. disables) the “disable while typing” option for this input.

`disable-while-trackpointing` (optional boolean)  
If `#t` (resp. `#f`), enables (resp. disables) the “disable while track-pointing” option for this input.

`tap` (optional boolean)  
Enables or disables the “tap” option, which allows clicking by tapping on a touchpad.

`extra-content` (default: `'()`)  
Lines to add to the input block. The value of this field must a list whose elements are either strings or G-expressions.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-output** <a href="#index-sway_002doutput" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`sway-output` records describe Sway outputs (see sway-output(5)). Available fields are:

`identifier` (default: `'*`)  
Identifier of the monitor. The field accepts symbols and strings. If the `identifier` is a symbol, it is inserted as is; if it is a string, it will be quoted in the configuration file.

`resolution` (optional string)  
This string defines the resolution of the monitor.

`position` (optional)  
The (optional) value of this field must be a `point`. Example:

``` lisp
(position
 (point (x 1920)
        (y 0)))
```

`background` (optional)  
The value of this field describes what wallpaper to use on this output. The field accepts the following types of values:

- a string,

- a G-expression,

- a file-like object,

- a pair. The first argument of this pair must be a string, a G-expression or a file-like object. The second element describes how the wallpaper will be displayed. It must be a symbol among `stretch`, `fill`, `fit`, `center` and `tile`.

  If the second element is not specified (*i.e.* when the value is not a pair), the `fill` mode will be used.

> **Note:** In order to use an SVG file, you must have `librsvg` in your profile (*e.g.* by adding it in the `packages` field of `sway-configuration`).

`extra-content` (default: `'()`)  
List defining additional lines to add to the output configuration block. Elements of the list must be either strings or G-expressions.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-border-color** <a href="#index-sway_002dborder_002dcolor" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`border`  
Color of the border.

`background`  
Color of the background.

`text`  
Color of the text.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-color** <a href="#index-sway_002dcolor" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`background` (optional string)  
Background color of the bar.

`statusline` (optional string)  
Text color of the status line.

`focused-background` (optional string)  
Background color of the bar on the currently focused monitor.

`focused-statusline` (optional string)  
Text color of the statusline on the currently focused monitor.

`focused-workspace` (optional `sway-border-color`)  
Color scheme for focused workspaces.

`active-workspace` (optional `sway-border-color`)  
Color scheme for active workspaces.

`inactive-workspace` (optional `sway-border-color`)  
Color scheme for inactive workspaces.

`urgent-workspace` (optional `sway-border-color`)  
Color scheme for workspaces containing “urgent windows”.

`binding-mode` (optional `sway-border-color`)  
Color scheme for the binding mode indicator.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-bar** <a href="#index-sway_002dbar" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Describes the Sway bar (see sway-bar(5)).

`identifier` (default: `'bar0`)  
Identifier of the bar. The value must be a symbol.

`position` (optional)  
Specify the position of the bar. Accepted values are `'top` or `'bottom`.

`hidden-state` (optional)  
Specify the appearance of the bar when it is hidden. Accepted values are `'hide` or `'show`.

`binding-mode-indicator` (optional)  
Boolean enabling or disabling the binding mode indicator.

`colors` (optional)  
An optional `sway-color` configuration record.

`status-command` (optional)  
This field accept strings, G-expressions and executable file-like values. The default value is a command (string) that prints the date and time every second.

Each line printed on `stdout` by this command (or script) will be displayed on the status area of the bar.

Below are a few examples using:

- a string: `"while date +'%Y-%m-%d %X'; do sleep 1; done"`,

- a G-exp:

  ``` lisp
  #~(string-append "while "
                   #$coreutils "/bin/date"
                   " +'%Y-%m-%d %X'; do sleep 1; done")
  ```

- an executable file:

  ``` lisp
  (program-file
   "sway-bar-status"
   #~(begin
       (use-modules (ice-9 format)
                    (srfi srfi-19))
       (let loop ()
         (let* ((date (date->string
                       (current-date)
                       "~d/~m/~Y (~a) • ~H:~M:~S")))
           (format #t "~a~%~!" date)
           (sleep 1)
           (loop)))))
  ```

`mouse-bindings` (default: `'()`)  
This field accepts an associative list. Keys are integers describing mouse events. Values are similar to that of key-bindings (except that “to-code” is not a valid option for mouse-bindings).

The module `(gnu home services sway)` exports constants `%ev-code-mouse-left`, `%ev-code-mouse-right` and `%ev-code-mouse-scroll-click` whose values are integers corresponding to left, right and scroll click respectively. For example, with `` (mouse-bindings `((,%ev-code-mouse-left . "exec $term"))) ``, left clicks in the status bar open the terminal (assuming that the variable `$term` is bound to a terminal).

<!-- -->

Data Type: **sway-mode** <a href="#index-sway_002dmode" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Describes a Sway mode (see sway(5)). For example, the following snippet defines the resize mode of the default Sway configuration:

``` example-preformatted
(sway-mode
 (mode-name "resize")
 (keybindings
  '(($left  . "resize shrink width 10px")
    ($right . "resize grow width 10px")
    ($down  . "resize grow height 10px")
    ($up    . "resize shrink height 10px")
    (Left   . "resize shrink width 10px")
    (Right  . "resize grow width 10px")
    (Down   . "resize grow height 10px")
    (Up     . "resize shrink height 10px")
    (Return . "mode \"default\"")
    (Escape . "mode \"default\""))))
```

`mode-name` (default: `"default"`)  
Name of the mode. This field accepts strings.

`keybindings` (default: `'()`)  
This field describes keybindings. The value is an association list. As above, keys are symbols and values are either strings, G-expressions or cons-cells.

`mouse-bindings` (default: `'()`)  
Ditto, but keys are mouse events (integers). Constants `%ev-code-mouse-*` described above can be used as helpers to define mouse bindings.

<span id="index-jellyfin" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `home-jellyfin-mpv-shim-service-type` in the `(gnu home services media)` module runs a cast client for the <a href="https://jellyfin.org/" class="uref">Jellyfin</a> media system.

To enable, add this to your home services:

``` lisp
(service home-jellyfin-mpv-shim-service-type)
```

The service starts only if `jellyfin-mpv-shim` has been configured with a remote server and credentials. This must be done manually, by launching `jellyfin-mpv-shim`. After configuring the server, the service will start automatically when you log in.

Variable: **home-jellyfin-mpv-shim-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002djellyfin_002dmpv_002dshim_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Type of the service which launches Jellyfin MPV Shim.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-jellyfin-mpv-shim-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002djellyfin_002dmpv_002dshim_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-jellyfin-mpv-shim-configuration` fields are:

`package` (default: `jellyfin-mpv-shim`) (type: package)  
The Jellyfin MPV Shim package to use.

#### 13.3.20 Networking Home Services <a href="#Networking-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

This section lists services somewhat networking-related that you may use with Guix Home.

#### Syncthing Service <a href="#Syncthing-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Syncthing_002c-file-synchronization-service-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-backup-service_002c-Syncthing-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services syncthing)` module provides a service to set up the <a href="Syncthing" class="uref">https://syncthing.net</a> continuous file backup service.

Variable: **home-syncthing-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dsyncthing_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for the `syncthing` daemon; it is the Home counterpart of the `syncthing-service-type` system service (see <a href="#Networking-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">syncthing-service-type</code></a>). The value for this service type is a `syncthing-configuration`.

Here is how you would set it up with the default configuration:

``` lisp
(service home-syncthing-service-type)
```

For a custom configuration, wrap you `syncthing-configuration` in `for-home`, as in this example:

``` lisp
(service home-syncthing-service-type
         (for-home
          (syncthing-configuration (logflags 5))))
```

For details about `syncthing-configuration`, check out the documentation of the system service (see <a href="#Networking-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">syncthing-service-type</code></a>).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.21 Secrets Home Services <a href="#Secrets-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(gnu home services secrets)` module provides services pertaining to storing secrets, notably including password managers.

#### Himitsu Services <a href="#Himitsu-Services" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<a href="https://himitsustore.org/" class="uref">Himitsu</a> is a daemon for storing arbitrary secrets encrypted by a single password. The daemon operates alongside a prompter, which asks the user for permission when an application requests a secret, and for the store password on first use in a session. Neither Himitsu nor its underlying cryptography library have been indepednently audited.

Variable: **home-himitsu-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This service provides the main Himitsu store daemon. It will not launch unless you have a store set up - run `himitsu-store -i` after the service is added to your profile to create it, and then `herd start himitsud` to restart the service. Configuration is as follows:

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-himitsu-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`package` (default: `himitsu`)  
Package to find `himitsud` in.

`notify-reuse` (optional)  
Interpreted shell command to run on application access to an already-approved secret.

`prompter` (default: `(wrap-himitsu-prompter (file-append hiprompt-gtk "/bin/hiprompt-gtk"))`)  
Path to a prompter binary. Defaults to `hiprompt-gtk`, the reference implementation. If your prompter is graphical, you should pass it through the provided `wrap-himitsu-prompter` procedure, which will autodetect a running display to prompt on, due to the Himitsu daemon starting before the display server is online.

`extra-options` (optional)  
List of extra strings or G-expressions to insert verbatim into the Himitsu configuration file. Each list element gets its own line.

Himitsu can be used through its command-line tool `hiq` or through any number of supporting services, providing compatability to other applications. Git credential support may be provided simply by adding the `himitsu-git` package to your profile, but other such supporting services are listed below:

Variable: **home-himitsu-ssh-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dssh_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This service provides an `ssh-agent` implementation that stores keys through Himitsu. You may interact with a running daemon through `hissh-import` and `hissh-export`.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-himitsu-ssh-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dssh_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`package` (default: `himitsu-ssh`)  
Package to find `hissh-agent` in.

`persist` (default: `'(session 300 refuse)`)  
List of options given when prompting to allow this service access to your list of keys. The option chosen decides how long `himitsu-ssh` has this access. Options can be either `'session` (access is retained until the daemon closes), `'refuse` (access is declined and the prompter will not ask again), `'skip` (ask again next use), or a numerical access timeout in seconds.

`disclose` (default: `'(skip session 300)`)  
List of options given when prompting to allow this service use of your secret keys. Has the same format as `persist`.

<!-- -->

Variable: **home-himitsu-secret-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dsecret_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This service provides a <a href="https://specifications.freedesktop.org/secret-service/latest/" class="uref">freedesktop Secret Service</a> implementation, allowing Himitsu to replace see <a href="#Desktop-Services" class="pxref">gnome-keyring-service-type</a> and see <a href="#Desktop-Services" class="pxref">kwallet-service-type</a>.

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-himitsu-secret-service-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dhimitsu_002dsecret_002dservice_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`package` (default: `himitsu-secret-service`)  
Package to find `hisecrets-agent` in.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 13.3.22 Miscellaneous Home Services <a href="#Miscellaneous-Home-Services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

This section lists Home services that lack a better place.

#### Beets Service <a href="#Beets-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Beets-service_002c-for-Home" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services music)` module provides the following service:

Variable: **home-beets-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dbeets_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
<a href="https://beets.io" class="uref">Beets</a> is a music file and metadata manager that can be used via its command-line interface, `beet`. Beets requires a YAML configuration file and this Guix Home service is to create such file.

The service can be used as follows:

``` lisp
(service home-beets-service-type
         (home-beets-configuration (directory "/home/alice/music")))
```

Additional options can be specified via the service wild-card field `extra-options`:

``` lisp
(service home-beets-service-type
         (home-beets-configuration
          (directory "/home/alice/music")
          (extra-options '("
import:
  move: yes"))))
```

#### Dictionary Service <a href="#Dictionary-Service-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-dictionary-service_002c-for-Home" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services dict)` module provides the following service:

Variable: **home-dicod-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002ddicod_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service that runs the `dicod` daemon, an implementation of DICT server (see <a href="https://puszcza.gnu.org.ua/software/dico/manual/dico.html#Dicod" data-manual="dico">Dicod</a> in GNU Dico Manual).

You can add `open localhost` to your `~/.dico` file to make `localhost` the default server for `dico` client (see <a href="https://puszcza.gnu.org.ua/software/dico/manual/dico.html#Initialization-File" data-manual="dico">Initialization File</a> in GNU Dico Manual).

This service is a direct mapping of the `dicod-service-type` system service (see <a href="#Miscellaneous-Services" class="pxref">Dictionary Service</a>). You can use it like this:

``` lisp
(service home-dicod-service-type)
```

You may specify a custom configuration by providing a `dicod-configuration` record, exactly like for `dicod-service-type`, but wrapping it in `for-home`:

``` lisp
(service home-dicod-service-type
         (for-home
          (dicod-configuration ...)))
```

#### ReadyMedia Service <a href="#ReadyMedia-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-ReadyMedia_002c-DLNA_002fUPnP-Service" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services upnp)` module provides a service to set up the <a href="https://minidlna.sourceforge.net/" class="uref">ReadyMedia</a> <span class="abbr acronym" title="Digital Living Network Alliance">DLNA</span> (Digital Living Network Alliance) <span class="abbr acronym" title="Universal Plug and Play">UPnP</span> (Universal Plug and Play) media server.

Variable: **home-readymedia-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dreadymedia_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the service type for the `minidlnad` daemon; it is the Home counterpart of the `readymedia-service-type` system service (see <a href="#Miscellaneous-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">readymedia-service-type</code></a>). The value for this service type is a `readymedia-configuration`.

The service can be used with a `readymedia-configuration` wrapped in `for-home` like this:

``` lisp
(service home-readymedia-service-type
         (for-home
          (readymedia-configuration
            (media-directories
             (list (readymedia-media-directory
                     (path "/path/to/media/audio")
                     (types '(A)))
                   (readymedia-media-directory
                     (path "/path/to/media/video")
                     (types '(V)))
                   (readymedia-media-directory
                     (path "/path/to/media/misc")))))))
```

For details about `readymedia-configuration`, check out the documentation of the system service (see <a href="#Miscellaneous-Services" class="pxref"><code class="code">readymedia-service-type</code></a>).

#### OCI backed services <a href="#OCI-backed-services-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-OCI_002dbacked_002c-for-Home" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services containers)` module provides the following service:

Variable: **home-oci-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002doci_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service that allows to manage your OCI containers with the same consistent interface you use for your other Home Shepherd services.

This service is a direct mapping of the `oci-service-type` system service (see <a href="#Miscellaneous-Services" class="pxref">OCI backed services</a>). You can use it like this:

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu services containers)
             (gnu home services containers))

(simple-service 'home-oci-provisioning
                home-oci-service-type
                (oci-extension
                  (volumes
                    (list
                      (oci-volume-configuration (name "prometheus"))
                      (oci-volume-configuration (name "grafana"))))
                  (networks
                    (list
                      (oci-network-configuration (name "monitoring"))))
                  (containers
                   (list
                    (oci-container-configuration
                     (network "monitoring")
                     (image
                      (oci-image
                        (repository "guile")
                        (tag "3")
                        (value (specifications->manifest '("guile")))
                        (pack-options '(#:symlinks (("/bin/guile" -> "bin/guile"))
                                        #:max-layers 2))))
                     (entrypoint "/bin/guile")
                     (command
                      '("-c" "(display \"hello!\n\")")))
                    (oci-container-configuration
                      (image "prom/prometheus")
                      (network "monitoring")
                      (ports
                       '(("9000" . "9000")
                         ("9090" . "9090")))
                      (volumes
                       (list
                        '(("prometheus" . "/var/lib/prometheus")))))
                    (oci-container-configuration
                      (image "grafana/grafana:10.0.1")
                      (network "monitoring")
                      (volumes
                       '(("grafana:/var/lib/grafana"))))))))
```

You may specify a custom configuration by providing a `oci-configuration` record, exactly like for `oci-service-type`, but wrapping it in `for-home`:

``` lisp
(use-modules (gnu services)
             (gnu services containers)
             (gnu home services containers))

(service home-oci-service-type
         (for-home
          (oci-configuration
           (runtime 'podman)
           (verbose? #t))))

(simple-service 'home-oci-provisioning
                home-oci-service-type
                (oci-extension
                  (volumes
                    (list
                      (oci-volume-configuration (name "prometheus"))
                      (oci-volume-configuration (name "grafana"))))
                  (networks
                    (list
                      (oci-network-configuration (name "monitoring"))))
                  (containers
                   (list
                    (oci-container-configuration
                     (network "monitoring")
                     (image
                      (oci-image
                        (repository "guile")
                        (tag "3")
                        (value (specifications->manifest '("guile")))
                        (pack-options '(#:symlinks (("/bin/guile" -> "bin/guile"))
                                        #:max-layers 2))))
                     (entrypoint "/bin/guile")
                     (command
                      '("-c" "(display \"hello!\n\")")))
                    (oci-container-configuration
                      (image "prom/prometheus")
                      (network "monitoring")
                      (ports
                       '(("9000" . "9000")
                         ("9090" . "9090")))
                      (volumes
                       (list
                        '(("prometheus" . "/var/lib/prometheus")))))
                    (oci-container-configuration
                      (image "grafana/grafana:10.0.1")
                      (network "monitoring")
                      (volumes
                       '(("grafana:/var/lib/grafana"))))))))
```

#### git-annex assistant Service <a href="#git_002dannex-assistant-Service" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-git_002dannex-assistant-service" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The `(gnu home services git-annex-assistant)` module provides a service to run the <a href="https://git-annex.branchable.com/assistant/" class="uref">git-annex assistant</a>.

Variable: **home-git-annex-assistant-service-type** <a href="#index-home_002dgit_002dannex_002dassistant_002dservice_002dtype" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the type of the service that runs the assistant. You must supply a `<home-git-annex-assistant-configuration>`.

The service runs one assistant for each directory provided. For example:

``` lisp
(service home-git-annex-assistant-service-type
         (home-git-annex-assistant-configuration
           (directories '("/path/to/foo" "/path/to/bar"))))
```

<!-- -->

Data Type: **home-git-annex-assistant-configuration** <a href="#index-home_002dgit_002dannex_002dassistant_002dconfiguration" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Available `home-git-annex-assistant-configuration` fields are:

`package` (default: `git-annex`) (type: package)  
Package that provides `git-annex`.

`directories` (default: `()`) (type: list-of-strings)  
List of directories.

### 13.4 Invoking `guix home` <a href="#Invoking-guix-home-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-guix-home" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Once you have written a home environment declaration (see <a href="#Declaring-the-Home-Environment" class="pxref">Declaring the Home Environment</a>, it can be *instantiated* using the `guix home` command. The synopsis is:

``` example-preformatted
guix home options... action file
```

`file` must be the name of a file containing a `home-environment` declaration. `action` specifies how the home environment is instantiated, but there are few auxiliary actions which don’t instantiate it. Currently the following values are supported:

`search`  
Display available home service type definitions that match the given regular expressions, sorted by relevance:

<span id="index-shell-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-shell_002dprofile" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-bash-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-zsh-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

``` example-preformatted
$ guix home search shell
name: home-shell-profile
location: gnu/home/services/shells.scm:100:2
extends: home-files
description: Create `~/.profile', which is used for environment initialization of POSIX compliant login shells.
+ This service type can be extended with a list of file-like objects.
relevance: 6

name: home-fish
location: gnu/home/services/shells.scm:640:2
extends: home-files home-profile
description: Install and configure Fish, the friendly interactive shell.
relevance: 3

name: home-zsh
location: gnu/home/services/shells.scm:290:2
extends: home-files home-profile
description: Install and configure Zsh.
relevance: 1

name: home-bash
location: gnu/home/services/shells.scm:508:2
extends: home-files home-profile
description: Install and configure GNU Bash.
relevance: 1

...
```

As for `guix search`, the result is written in `recutils` format, which makes it easy to filter the output (see <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org/recutils/latest/en/recutils.html#Top" data-manual="recutils">GNU recutils databases</a> in GNU recutils manual).

<span id="index-container_002c-for-guix-home-1"></span>`container` <a href="#index-container_002c-for-guix-home-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Spawn a shell in an isolated environment—a *container*—containing your home as specified by `file`.

For example, this is how you would start an interactive shell in a container with your home:

``` example-preformatted
guix home container config.scm
```

This is a throw-away container where you can lightheartedly fiddle with files; any changes made within the container, any process started—all this disappears as soon as you exit that shell.

As with `guix shell`, several options control that container:

`--network`  
`-N`  
Enable networking within the container (it is disabled by default).

`--expose=``source``[=``target``]`  
`--share=``source``[=``target``]`  
As with `guix shell`, make directory `source` of the host system available as `target` inside the container—read-only if you pass `--expose`, and writable if you pass `--share` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-shell" class="pxref"><samp class="option">--expose</samp> and <samp class="option">--share</samp></a>).

Additionally, you can run a command in that container, instead of spawning an interactive shell. For instance, here is how you would check which Shepherd services are started in a throw-away home container:

``` example-preformatted
guix home container config.scm -- herd status
```

The command to run in the container must come after `--` (double hyphen).

<span id="index-editing_002c-service-type-definition-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-service-type-definition_002c-editing-1"></span>`edit` <a href="#index-service-type-definition_002c-editing-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Edit or view the definition of the given Home service types.

For example, the command below opens your editor, as specified by the `EDITOR` environment variable, on the definition of the `home-mcron` service type:

``` example-preformatted
guix home edit home-mcron
```

`reconfigure`  
Build the home environment described in `file`, and switch to it. Switching means that the activation script will be evaluated and (in basic scenario) symlinks to configuration files generated from `home-environment` declaration will be created in `~`. If the file with the same path already exists in home folder it will be moved to `~/``timestamp``-guix-home-legacy-configs-backup`, where `timestamp` is a current UNIX epoch time.

> **Note:** It is highly recommended to run `guix pull` once before you run `guix home reconfigure` for the first time (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-pull" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix pull</code></a>).

This effects all the configuration specified in `file`. The command starts Shepherd services specified in `file` that are not currently running; if a service is currently running, this command will arrange for it to be upgraded the next time it is stopped (e.g. by `herd stop ``service` or `herd restart ``service`).

This command creates a new generation whose number is one greater than the current generation (as reported by `guix home list-generations`). If that generation already exists, it will be overwritten. This behavior mirrors that of `guix package` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-package" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix package</code></a>).

<span id="index-provenance-tracking_002c-of-the-home-environment" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Upon completion, the new home is deployed under `~/.guix-home`. This directory contains *provenance meta-data*: the list of channels in use (see <a href="#Channels" class="pxref">Channels</a>) and `file` itself, when available. You can view the provenance information by running:

``` example-preformatted
guix home describe
```

This information is useful should you later want to inspect how this particular generation was built. In fact, assuming `file` is self-contained, you can later rebuild generation `n` of your home environment with:

``` example-preformatted
guix time-machine \
  -C /var/guix/profiles/per-user/USER/guix-home-n-link/channels.scm -- \
  home reconfigure \
  /var/guix/profiles/per-user/USER/guix-home-n-link/configuration.scm
```

You can think of it as some sort of built-in version control! Your home is not just a binary artifact: *it carries its own source*.

> **Note:** If you’re using Guix System, <a href="#guix_002dhome_002dservice_002dtype" class="ref"><code class="code">guix-home-service-type</code></a>, on how to embed your home configuration in your system configuration such that `guix system reconfigure` deploys both your system and your home.

<span id="index-home-generations"></span>`switch-generation` <a href="#index-home-generations" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Switch to an existing home generation. This action atomically switches the home profile to the specified home generation.

The target generation can be specified explicitly by its generation number. For example, the following invocation would switch to home generation 7:

``` example-preformatted
guix home switch-generation 7
```

The target generation can also be specified relative to the current generation with the form `+N` or `-N`, where `+3` means “3 generations ahead of the current generation,” and `-1` means “1 generation prior to the current generation.” When specifying a negative value such as `-1`, you must precede it with `--` to prevent it from being parsed as an option. For example:

``` example-preformatted
guix home switch-generation -- -1
```

This action will fail if the specified generation does not exist.

<span id="index-rolling-back-3"></span>`roll-back` <a href="#index-rolling-back-3" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Switch to the preceding home generation. This is the inverse of `reconfigure`, and it is exactly the same as invoking `switch-generation` with an argument of `-1`.

<span id="index-saving-space-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-deleting-home-generations"></span>`delete-generations` <a href="#index-deleting-home-generations" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Delete home generations, making them candidates for garbage collection (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-gc" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix gc</code></a>, for information on how to run the “garbage collector”).

This works in the same way as ‘`guix package --delete-generations`’ (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-package" class="pxref"><samp class="option">--delete-generations</samp></a>). With no arguments, all home generations but the current one are deleted:

``` example-preformatted
guix home delete-generations
```

You can also select the generations you want to delete. The example below deletes all the home generations that are more than two months old:

``` example-preformatted
guix home delete-generations 2m
```

`build`  
Build the derivation of the home environment, which includes all the configuration files and programs needed. This action does not actually install anything.

`describe`  
Describe the current home generation: its file name, as well as provenance information when available.

To show installed packages in the current home generation’s profile, the `--list-installed` flag is provided, with the same syntax that is used in `guix package --list-installed` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-package" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix package</code></a>). For instance, the following command shows a table of all the packages with “emacs” in their name that are installed in the current home generation’s profile:

``` example-preformatted
guix home describe --list-installed=emacs
```

`list-generations`  
List a summary of each generation of the home environment available on disk, in a human-readable way. This is similar to the `--list-generations` option of `guix package` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-package" class="pxref">Invoking <code class="command">guix package</code></a>).

Optionally, one can specify a pattern, with the same syntax that is used in `guix package --list-generations`, to restrict the list of generations displayed. For instance, the following command displays generations that are up to 10 days old:

``` example-preformatted
guix home list-generations 10d
```

The `--list-installed` flag may also be specified, with the same syntax that is used in `guix home describe`. This may be helpful if trying to determine when a package was added to the home profile.

`import`  
Generate a *home environment* from the packages in the default profile and configuration files found in the user’s home directory. The configuration files will be copied to the specified directory, and a `home-configuration.scm` will be populated with the home environment. Note that not every home service that exists is supported (see <a href="#Home-Services" class="pxref">Home Services</a>).

``` example-preformatted
$ guix home import ~/guix-config
guix home: '/home/alice/guix-config' populated with all the Home configuration files
```

And there’s more! `guix home` also provides the following sub-commands to visualize how the services of your home environment relate to one another:

<span id="index-service-extension-graph_002c-of-a-home-environment"></span>`extension-graph` <a href="#index-service-extension-graph_002c-of-a-home-environment" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Emit to standard output the *service extension graph* of the home environment defined in `file` (see <a href="#Service-Composition" class="pxref">Service Composition</a>, for more information on service extensions). By default the output is in Dot/Graphviz format, but you can choose a different format with `--graph-backend`, as with `guix graph` (see <a href="#Invoking-guix-graph" class="pxref"><samp class="option">--backend</samp></a>):

The command:

``` example-preformatted
guix home extension-graph file | xdot -
```

shows the extension relations among services.

<span id="index-Shepherd-dependency-graph_002c-for-a-home-environment"></span>`shepherd-graph` <a href="#index-Shepherd-dependency-graph_002c-for-a-home-environment" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Emit to standard output the *dependency graph* of shepherd services of the home environment defined in `file`. See <a href="#Shepherd-Services" class="xref">Shepherd Services</a>, for more information and for an example graph.

Again, the default output format is Dot/Graphviz, but you can pass `--graph-backend` to select a different one.

`options` can contain any of the common build options (see <a href="#Common-Build-Options" class="pxref">Common Build Options</a>). In addition, `options` can contain one of the following:

`--expression=``expr`  
`-e ``expr`  
Consider the home-environment `expr` evaluates to. This is an alternative to specifying a file which evaluates to a home environment.

`--allow-downgrades`  
Instruct `guix home reconfigure` to allow system downgrades.

Just like `guix system`, `guix home reconfigure`, by default, prevents you from downgrading your home to older or unrelated revisions compared to the channel revisions that were used to deploy it—those shown by `guix home describe`. Using `--allow-downgrades` allows you to bypass that check, at the risk of downgrading your home—be careful!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 14 Documentation <a href="#Documentation-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-documentation_002c-searching-for" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-searching-for-documentation" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Documentation for Guix itself is <a href="https://guix.gnu.org/manual/devel" class="uref">available online</a> and documentation for a number of “Guix-adjacent packages” is available from <a href="https://doc.guix.gnu.org" class="uref">the Documentation Center</a>. These provide an easy way to browse documentation online, but you can also access it locally on your computer, as we will see below.

<span id="index-Info_002c-documentation-format" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-man-pages" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-manual-pages" class="index-entry-id"></span>

In most cases packages installed with Guix come with documentation. There are two main documentation formats: “Info”, a browsable hypertext format used for GNU software, and “manual pages” (or “man pages”), the linear documentation format traditionally found on Unix. Info manuals are accessed with the `info` command or with Emacs, and man pages are accessed using `man`.

You can look for documentation of software installed on your system by keyword. For example, the following command searches for information about “TLS” in Info manuals:

``` example-preformatted
$ info -k TLS
"(emacs)Network Security" -- STARTTLS
"(emacs)Network Security" -- TLS
"(gnutls)Core TLS API" -- gnutls_certificate_set_verify_flags
"(gnutls)Core TLS API" -- gnutls_certificate_set_verify_function
...
```

The command below searches for the same keyword in man pages<a href="#FOOT40" id="DOCF40" class="footnote"><sup>40</sup></a>:

``` example-preformatted
$ man -k TLS
SSL (7)              - OpenSSL SSL/TLS library
certtool (1)         - GnuTLS certificate tool
...
```

These searches are purely local to your computer so you have the guarantee that documentation you find corresponds to what you have actually installed, you can access it off-line, and your privacy is respected.

Once you have these results, you can view the relevant documentation by running, say:

``` example-preformatted
$ info "(gnutls)Core TLS API"
```

or:

``` example-preformatted
$ man certtool
```

Info manuals contain sections and indices as well as hyperlinks like those found in Web pages. The `info` reader (see <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/texinfo/manual/info-stnd/info-stnd.html#Top" data-manual="info-stnd">Info reader</a> in Stand-alone GNU Info) and its Emacs counterpart (see <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_mono/emacs.html#Misc-Help" data-manual="emacs">Misc Help</a> in The GNU Emacs Manual) provide intuitive key bindings to navigate manuals. See <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_mono/info.html#Getting-Started" data-manual="info">Getting Started</a> in Info: An Introduction, for an introduction to Info navigation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15 Platforms <a href="#Platforms-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The packages and systems built by Guix are intended, like most computer programs, to run on a CPU with a specific instruction set, and under a specific operating system. Those programs are often also targeting a specific kernel and system library. Those constraints are captured by Guix in `platform` records.

- [`platform` Reference](#platform-Reference)
- [Supported Platforms](#Supported-Platforms)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 15.1 `platform` Reference <a href="#platform-Reference-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `platform` data type describes a *platform*: an <span class="abbr acronym" title="instruction set architecture">ISA</span> (instruction set architecture), combined with an operating system and possibly additional system-wide settings such as the <span class="abbr acronym" title="application binary interface">ABI</span> (application binary interface).

Data Type: **platform** <a href="#index-platform" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
This is the data type representing a platform.

`target`  
This field specifies the platform’s GNU triplet as a string (see <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/autoconf/manual/autoconf.html#Specifying-Target-Triplets" data-manual="autoconf">GNU configuration triplets</a> in Autoconf).

`system`  
This string is the system type as it is known to Guix and passed, for instance, to the `--system` option of most commands.

It usually has the form `"``cpu``-``kernel``"`, where `cpu` is the target CPU and `kernel` the target operating system kernel.

It can be for instance `"aarch64-linux"` or `"armhf-linux"`. You will encounter system types when you perform native builds (see <a href="#Native-Builds" class="pxref">Native Builds</a>).

`linux-architecture` (default: `#false`)  
This optional string field is only relevant if the kernel is Linux. In that case, it corresponds to the ARCH variable used when building Linux, `"mips"` for instance.

`rust-target` (default: `#false`)  
This optional string field is used to determine which rust target is best supported by this platform. For example, the base level system targeted by `armhf-linux` system is closest to `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf`.

`glibc-dynamic-linker`  
This field is the name of the GNU C Library dynamic linker for the corresponding system, as a string. It can be `"/lib/ld-linux-armhf.so.3"`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 15.2 Supported Platforms <a href="#Supported-Platforms-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `(guix platforms …)` modules export the following variables, each of which is bound to a `platform` record.

Variable: **armv7-linux** <a href="#index-armv7_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting ARM v7 CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **aarch64-linux** <a href="#index-aarch64_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting ARM v8 CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **loongarch64-linux** <a href="#index-loongarch64_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting loongarch 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **mips64-linux** <a href="#index-mips64_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting MIPS little-endian 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **powerpc-linux** <a href="#index-powerpc_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting PowerPC big-endian 32-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **powerpc64le-linux** <a href="#index-powerpc64le_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting PowerPC little-endian 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **riscv64-linux** <a href="#index-riscv64_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting RISC-V 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **i686-linux** <a href="#index-i686_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting x86 CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **x86_64-linux** <a href="#index-x86_005f64_002dlinux" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting x86 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux.

<!-- -->

Variable: **x86_64-linux-x32** <a href="#index-x86_005f64_002dlinux_002dx32" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting x86 64-bit CPU running GNU/Linux with the run-time using the X32 ABI.

<!-- -->

Variable: **i686-mingw** <a href="#index-i686_002dmingw" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting x86 CPU running Windows, with run-time support from MinGW.

<!-- -->

Variable: **x86_64-mingw** <a href="#index-x86_005f64_002dmingw" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<!-- -->

Variable: **i586-gnu** <a href="#index-i586_002dgnu" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting x86 CPU running GNU/Hurd (also referred to as “GNU”).

<!-- -->

Variable: **avr** <a href="#index-avr" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Platform targeting AVR CPUs without an operating system, with run-time support from AVR Libc.

<!-- -->

Variable: **or1k-elf** <a href="#index-or1k_002delf" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Variable: **xtensa-ath9k-elf** <a href="#index-xtensa_002dath9k_002delf" class="copiable-link">¶</a>
